newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers condemn improper gifts to local candidates.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers condemn improper gifts to local candidates.

text.p: Delegates to the American Bar Association's annual meeting Wednesday adopted a policy opposing the practice of paying political contributions to elected state and local government officials in return for lucrative municipal finance work.
They also called for a new committee to propose possible solutions by August 1998.
"This is a significant first step," said Michael Cardozo, the president of New York City's bar association, the first lawyers' group to urge the ABA to ban the policy, dubbed pay-to-play.
Cardozo said now that the policy has been enacted, lawyers must translate it into a meaningful set of rules.

The $1.3 trillion dollar municipal bond market has been rocked with allegations that Wall Street firms that underwrite bonds for huge highway, airport, and road financings get the jobs partly because they make contributions to influential mayors, county commissioners and other elected politicians.
Exasperated by the practice, major Wall Street players in 1994 volunteered to stop making such contributions.
The landmark agreement was strongly endorsed by Arthur Levitt, chairman of Wall Street's Washington watchdog -- the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Levitt then launched a new campaign to get the lawyers who work for the securities firms and state and local governments on bond financings to come up with their own pay-to-play ban.
Lawyers for months opposed the move, saying it would abridge their constitutional right to freedom of speech and that regulators have no proof that lawyers engage in "pay-to-play."
But last year, Cardozo's group, the Association of the Bar of the City of New York, declared pay-to-play a major problem for its members and voted to ban it.
The group then urged the ABA to follow suit.
After months of wrangling over language, ABA delegates voted Wednesday to condemn the practice.
It also called on state and local legislatures, judges and bar associations nationwide to act.
They should adopt laws and regulations that discourage pay-to-play, the new ABA policy says.
"I applaud the bar today for taking an important step in the right direction by condemning pay-to-play," SEC's Levitt said.
"Tomorrow we'll begin a national campaign against pay-to-play by working in every state to convince state and local bar associations to eliminate this odious practice," Levitt added.
